text: Ukraine does not publish a per-effector breakdown of drone kills, and the Ukrainian Air Force's "downed/suppressed" total mixes kills with diversions by electronic warfare.

In autumn 2022 Ukraine's answer to the first Shaheds was improvised: small teams with machine guns, MANPADS, thermal sights and laser pointers, cued by a central air picture, tablets and residents' Telegram reports.
Through 2023 and the first half of 2024 mobile fire groups became the main Shahed killer; the Ukrainian Air Force commander said they made more than 80% of Shahed kills in the first half of 2024.

observations.subject: mobile fire groups' share of Shahed kills

text: From 2025 Shaheds flew above 2 km, out of machine-gun reach.
Interceptor drones took over from mobile fire groups, rising from about 10–25% of Shahed kills in winter 2025–26 to about 40–50% in spring 2026.
From mid-2026 the jet Gerans outran both Ukraine's guns and its propeller interceptor drones.
In 2022 Ukrainian mobile fire group crews got about 10 minutes' warning to reach their position.

observations.subject: mobile fire group alert to position

metric_new.label: Warning lead time before an engagement

text: A 2026 Frontliner report found that mobile fire group crews were often warned only once they could already hear the drone, too late to engage.
Ukrainian interceptor drone crews describe a window of a few minutes between a Shahed appearing on radar and leaving their range.
A Merops crew says a calibrated radar with a good operator gives the best target data, while flight-path programmes can be off by about a kilometre.

metric_new.label: Position error of a target cue

text: A Merops crew says the earlier Ukrainian interceptor drone's camera had to get within about 200 m before it could find the target.

observations.subject: earlier interceptor drone camera search distance

text: A Gepard kills a Shahed with "a handful" of 35 mm rounds at about $600 each, so a few thousand dollars a kill.

metric_new.label: Defender cost per aerial target killed

text: Skynex fires about 10 programmable AHEAD rounds per target, out to about 4 km.
Gepard and Skynex are point defences that Shaheds flying above 2–3 km can overfly.

observations.subject: Shahed altitude that overflies Gepard and Skynex

text: A Ukrainian ZU-23-2 gunner put his own hit rate at "every hundredth shot".
The Sting interceptor drone costs about $2,000 and flies at about 280–340 km/h, depending on the source.
A Sting operator flies the interceptor onto a radar dot over a video link, and from 2026 onboard AI makes the terminal lock.
Fog and cloud defeat interceptor drones' cameras: one crew logged ten launches in a night and found no Shahed.

observations.subject: interceptor launches in one night with no Shahed found

text: Russia answered Ukrainian interceptor drones with rear-view cameras and evasive manoeuvres on Shaheds, and then with jet Gerans.
On 4 July 2025, 208 of 539 Russian drones and decoys were "diverted", most likely by Ukrainian jamming.
Reuters says Ukrainian EW can neutralise nearly half of a Russian drone attack on some nights.

observations.subject: share of an attack neutralised by EW on some nights

text: Russia climbed the CRPA ladder from 8 to 16 antenna elements on Shaheds by March 2025.
Ukrainian GNSS spoofing moved civilians' phones into Russian time zones.
The Tryzub laser was shown in April 2025 and again in May 2026 with claimed ranges of 3 km against drones and 5 km against aircraft, aimed by hand with a joystick.
In July 2026 the Deputy Commander-in-Chief said the Tryzub laser kills FPVs and would be ready against Shaheds "in two to three months".
No documented Shahed kill by a laser was found, and no high-power microwave or EMP system against Shaheds was found at all.
In October 2022 a Ukrainian mobile fire group had 4–5 people, usually with 2 MANPADS launchers (Igla), a radio and a vehicle.

observations.subject: MANPADS launchers per mobile fire group

text: In October 2022 the National Guard of Ukraine alone had about 130 mobile fire groups among more than 250 firing groups.

In November 2022 Mykolaiv had dozens of anti-drone units of about six people each, drawn from the police, army, territorial defence and the National Guard, rotating night shifts between firing points chosen to reduce civilian risk.

In November 2022 Mykolaiv's anti-drone teams used heavy machine guns, including a .50 cal taken from a destroyed Russian tank and mounted on a convertible, plus thermal sensors, a laser to illuminate targets and a WWII flare gun.

In December 2022 Ukraine's drone hunters were small, ad hoc, dispersed teams with small arms and machine guns on pickups and cars; one UAZ-452 van carried twin PKT 7.62 mm guns on a local mount, and MANPADS on vehicles were the exception.
In December 2022 Ukrainian drone-hunter teams used a gun-like thermal sensor to spot a drone, then a laser to mark the target for the other shooters.

In February 2023 Kyiv's "Shahed and missile hunters" rode in off-road passenger cars with heavy machine guns, thermal imagers and laser target designators, and were ready for combat in no more than one minute.

observations.subject: Kyiv mobile group readiness for combat

text: In November 2023 Ukrainian mobile teams used SUVs with a tripod and Mistral, light vehicles with PKT, DShKM, Maxim or Browning guns and workshop-made anti-aircraft sights, trucks with ZU-23-2, upgraded Zastava M75 20 mm guns with HikVision thermal optics feeding a tablet, and mobile EW teams with Nota; Stinger was also used.
In November 2023 National Guard Spaceray searchlights detected drones to about 2 km, even when the drones were painted matte black.

In January 2024 Ukrainian anti-Shahed crews received an M2HB Browning with a "special digital" thermal sight with automatic target acquisition, a Strela-2 with a thermal sight, and Igla launchers with Guide TK 431 thermal imagers, 100 of which were bought by the Prytula Foundation.

observations.subject: Guide TK 431 thermal imagers bought by the Prytula Foundation

text: In April 2024 several Ukrainian mobile groups tested new Ukrainian searchlights as part of a system with a laser and a thermal sight to find and track targets and adjust fire.

In June 2024 Air Force commander Oleshchuk described "thousands of servicemen who go to firing positions almost every night" in mobile fire groups, with small arms, AA guns and MANPADS upgraded with night vision, thermal imagers, laser pointers, searchlights, EW devices and software.

cites.quote: thousands of servicemen who go to firing positions almost every night

text: In September 2025 a Ukrainian mobile fire group officially had three soldiers, two on duty at the observed position, each cross-trained to fire alone.

In September 2025 Ukrainian mobile fire groups used ZU-23 guns on GAZ-66 trucks fitted with the Ukrainian ZIR+ system (optics, rangefinder, thermal imager, camera), and pickups with Brownings on the Oskil.
In October 2025 the 68th Jaeger Brigade's anti-drone teams of three rotated every two hours from underground, camouflaged positions with a spare position, because FPVs hunt the first position.
A 68th Jaeger Brigade gunner gave the Browning a range of about 4 km maximum and about 2 km effective; the team also used a large-calibre rifle against FPVs and an electronic thermal sight.

In February–March 2026 Ukrainian mobile fire groups used pickups with machine guns and crews of 2–3 that moved often; the Browning M2 with thermal optics was "considered the most effective", with Igla or Stinger kept for faster targets.
In early 2026 Ukrainian mobile fire group crews wanted interceptor drones of their own.
The Chaika and Chaika-M VR simulators, codified for the Ukrainian Armed Forces in November 2025, train mobile fire group crews with virtual Igla, Stinger, DShK and M2 at night, with a searchlight.

From June 2025 a Cabinet of Ministers pilot lets volunteer formations of territorial communities form air-defence groups, subordinate to Territorial Defence commanders and, for air-defence tasks, to the Air Force Command.
Members of Ukraine's volunteer air-defence groups may use small arms, strike UAVs, private manned aircraft, EW and AI systems, and must be exempt from mobilisation and trained.
In October 2022 Ukrainian mobile fire groups were cued by "centralised information, what is flying, where and where from".

cites.quote: Centralised information, what is flying, where and where from

text: In November 2022 Ukrainian drone hunters were cued by tablets showing approaching Shaheds and by residents' Telegram reports, then by a thermal sensor and a laser on site, and had "roughly 10 minutes" to reach a firing position after an alert.

metric_new.label: Warning lead time before an engagement

text: In November 2023 acoustic sensors fed a single database through monitoring points, and a detection was passed "across units until one can engage it"; Come Back Alive planned radio kits for air-picture data and target designation.

cites.quote: across units until one can engage it

text: In October 2025 one gunner in an underground command post watched a tablet receiving "data on all detected aerial targets", and crews aimed with lead because the sound lags the drone.

cites.quote: data on all detected aerial targets

text: In February 2026 Ukrainian mobile fire group crews "often receive warnings only after they already hear the drone", by which time the drone is in the strike zone or leaves it within seconds.

cites.quote: often receive warnings only after they already hear the drone

text: In February 2026 an expert proposed 30 kg vehicle radars giving mobile fire groups coordinates, speed and altitude, and a planned "anti-drone dome" of radars and acoustic sensors would give azimuth and time of arrival.

The 2022 crews' working cue of about 10 minutes, the 2025 crews' about 40 minutes' launch notice and the 2026 complaint of late warning measure different things: a launch warning tells a crew when to man its position, while a track tells it where to point the gun, and the 2026 complaint is about the track.
The Ukrainian Air Force gave machine guns an effective engagement altitude of up to 1 km in 2026.

metric_new.label: Maximum effective engagement altitude of a weapon

text: A Ukrainian gunner gave the Browning M2 a reach of about 4 km maximum and about 2 km effective.
The ZU-23-2 has an effective range of 2,500 m.
The Spaceray searchlight detects drones to about 2 km.
In 2023 Shaheds were described as "low-flying slow Shaheds".
By May 2025 Shaheds flew above 2 km, then dived onto the target.
In September 2025 Shaheds flew at 1,500–2,800 m, sometimes 3,000 m.
In July 2025 Shaheds flew either very low, up to about 200 m, or at 1,000–4,000 m.
Reuters reported in 2026 that Shahed speed rose from about 170 km/h to over 200 km/h.
Gwara gave the Shahed's speed as about 200 km/h in 2025.
Ihnat said in May 2025 that at above 2 km Shaheds "become more visible to our radars" but stay "out of reach of small arms, heavy machine guns, and mobile fire teams".

cites.quote: out of reach of small arms, heavy machine guns, and mobile fire teams

text: By February 2026 Ihnat described Shaheds flying either above mobile fire group reach or low along reservoirs and river beds, on routes planned from Russian satellite, signals and weather intelligence.
Between 13 September and 21 October 2022, 223 Shahed-136s were destroyed over Ukraine, much of it credited to mobile units, though military reports rarely say which means killed a drone.
On 20 October 2022 the National Guard of Ukraine made 2 of 14 Shahed kills.

observations.subject: Shahed kills by the National Guard

text: Militarnyi reported 440 Shahed-136s recorded over Ukraine in 2022, with 78 hits on targets (about 18%).
One Mykolaiv anti-drone team had shot down 3 Shaheds by early November 2022.
Ihnat said mobile fire groups made about 40% of the night's kills on 25 November 2023, when 74 of 75 Shaheds were downed; earlier their share had been up to 50%, but against only 5–10 drones.

observations.subject: mobile fire groups' share of one night's Shahed kills
mobile fire groups' share on earlier nights of 5–10 drones

text: In December 2023 Ihnat said mobile fire groups shoot down "most" Shaheds: 2,900 of 3,700 since September 2022, about 78% overall (computed).

observations.subject: Shaheds downed by mobile fire groups since Sep 2022
mobile fire groups' share of Shahed kills

text: Air Force commander Oleshchuk said mobile fire groups made more than 80% of Shahed kills from 1 January to 26 June 2024, when 2,277 Shaheds were launched and about 86% destroyed.

observations.subject: mobile fire groups' share of Shahed kills

text: In September 2025 a ZU-23 gunner estimated that "every hundredth shot hits".
Compiled Ukrainian Air Force reports show roughly 95% of Shaheds shot down in the same 2022 months for which Militarnyi gives a Shahed hit share of about 18%, so the two figures do not match.

observations.subject: Shaheds shot down in compiled Air Force reports, 2022

text: The 2022 Shahed hit share and the Air Force shoot-down share count different things (hits on targets against drones not reported shot down), and neither is independent.
Gerbera decoys reveal Ukrainian mobile fire group positions when fired on, which can bring Russian strikes; crews use red rather than white light.
A Ukrainian brigade's gunners describe Russia sending one Shahed ahead to scout for firing groups, then sending others around their positions, and they hold fire without visual confirmation.

Beskrestnov reported "another hit by a guided Shahed" on a Ukrainian mobile fire group crew while it engaged a different Shahed, and told commanders to plan camouflage and a course of action in advance.

cites.quote: another hit by a guided Shahed

text: Near the front, Shaheds carrying FPVs or mines hunt vehicles, and an Igla was seen attached to a Shahed.

In September 2025 "readiness number one" sent all Ukrainian mobile fire groups to their positions when Shaheds were launched, giving about 40 minutes from launch to arrival; crews followed Telegram and maps, and positions were moved to the corridors used most often.

metric_new.label: Warning lead time before an engagement

text: The Ukrainian Air Force gave MANPADS an effective range of up to 4 km and an effective operating altitude of about 2 km.

metric_new.label: Maximum effective engagement altitude of a weapon

text: Ukraine had about 80 Gepards plus ex-Jordanian Cheetahs in July 2025.
In June 2026 Belgium was refurbishing 15 more Gepards for Ukraine.
Gepards have been repaired in Ukraine since August 2025.
The Gepard has twin radar-cued 35 mm Oerlikon guns firing up to 1,100 rounds a minute, engages targets up to 3 km altitude and fires "from a few kilometers away".

metric_new.label: Maximum effective engagement altitude of a weapon

text: Gepard operators and a developer say bursts of 7–11 rounds often suffice to kill a Shahed and the average is 20–30 rounds per target, and once several drones fell to one burst.

observations.subject: Gepard rounds per Shahed, often sufficient

text: David Axe wrote that a Gepard needs "a handful" of rounds per Shahed.
In June 2026 one Gepard crew downed 17 drones in one night over Khmelnytskyi oblast, with seconds between targets; its commander has 39 kills in all.
Germany paid $181m for 300,000 new Gepard rounds after sending its own stocks to Ukraine, then ordered 180,000 more.
A 35 mm Gepard round costs about $600, a figure relayed from Forbes.
Skynex has four towed 35 mm Revolver Mk3 guns (1,000 rounds a minute, 4 km reach), a sensor unit and a command post on the Skymaster battle-management system.
Skynex has been in use in Ukraine since spring 2023, and two systems were reported by April 2024.
Skynex uses about 10 AHEAD rounds per Shahed, each bursting ahead of the target with 152 tungsten pellets; in one video the first round killed.
RBC-Ukraine, via the Kyiv Independent, put Skynex's cost per target at "just over $4,000" in 2024.

metric_new.label: Defender cost per aerial target killed

text: drone-warfare.com derived about €1,120 per AHEAD round from a Romanian contract, so about $12,900 per 10-round Skynex burst, which disagrees with the reported cost per target of just over $4,000.

metric_new.label: Defender cost per aerial target killed

text: A Skynex battery commander reported about 35 Shaheds and 2 cruise missiles downed by one battery, with 12 targets in one engagement.

observations.subject: Shaheds downed by one Skynex battery
cruise missiles downed by one Skynex battery

text: According to an internal report, on 1 April 2026 three of eight Skynex guns at one site failed within minutes and a Shahed got through.

observations.subject: Skynex guns failed at one site

text: The ZU-23-2 with the ZIR+ system is a twin 23 mm gun; ZIR+ adds optics, a rangefinder, a thermal imager and a camera, the effective range is 2,500 m, and it would suit the lower Shaheds of earlier years better.
Ukraine's upgraded Zastava M75 20×110 mm guns have thermal and IR optics feeding the gunner's tablet.
Other guns and short-range systems named against Shaheds at low and medium altitude include Slinger, Vampire and Avenger.
In 2022 MANPADS were the Ukrainian mobile fire groups' main weapon.
Later Ukrainian MANPADS were kept for targets too fast or too high for the guns, such as jets and missiles.
Thermal sights were added to Ukrainian Strela-2 and Igla MANPADS.
MANPADS' stated reach is up to 4 km, with an effective altitude of about 2 km.

metric_new.label: Maximum effective engagement altitude of a weapon

text: Ukrainian Mi-8 and Mi-24 crews with door and turret machine guns claim more than 3,200 Shaheds from August 2024 to August 2025.
Ukrainian helicopter crews downed more than 440 Shaheds in May 2026.
Ukrainian helicopters claim up to 40% of drones in their zones.

observations.subject: helicopters' share of drones in their zones

text: Ground radar gives Ukrainian helicopter crews the first coordinates; from mid-2024 an unarmed H125 or H225 with a FLIR UltraFORCE 350 turret tracks the drone at night and guides the Mi-8 or Mi-24 gunship into position, and the pair try to bring the debris down in open country.
On their own, Mi-8 and Mi-24 gunships are "far less effective" against Shaheds at night or in poor visibility.
Russia answered Ukrainian helicopters with Shaheds carrying an R-60 missile (December 2025) or an Igla-S or Verba MANPADS in its tube, fired by an operator watching an onboard camera.
TWZ found no evidence that a MANPADS- or missile-armed Shahed had yet hit an aircraft and called the combination's effectiveness "questionable".
A Ukrainian MiG-29 pilot downed three drones on 12 October 2022, and debris from a fifth wounded him before he ejected.
In June 2025 F-16 pilot Lt. Col. Ustymenko downed seven targets and was killed when the last one's blast likely damaged his jet.
By June 2025 three of the four F-16s Ukraine had lost had gone down on air-defence patrols during Russian raids.
From December 2025 Ukrainian F-16s carried Sniper pods and laser-guided APKWS II rockets, about $30,000–31,000 each, up to 28 or more per sortie, against about 6 air-to-air missiles.
The first footage of an APKWS kill on a Shahed appeared in February 2026.
Reuters puts an F-16's haul at up to 10 Shaheds a night.
Against jet Gerans, Ihnat says fighters or surface-to-air missiles are needed.
Reuters gave the Sting interceptor a speed of 280 km/h and a reach of about 37 km in March 2026.
Wild Hornets gave the Sting a speed of over 315 km/h in 2025.
A maker figure relayed by MiGFlug gives the Sting a speed of 343 km/h.
A Sting interceptor costs about $2,000–2,500.
Radar finds the Shahed, the Sting is launched toward it, and a pilot flies it in over a video link with a thermal camera; FPV pilots learn to fly the Sting in 3–4 days.

SkyFall's P1-SUN interceptor costs about $1,000; the pilot flies it until the target's shape is clear, hands over to auto-targeting (a green box), then commits to the strike, and the targeting was trained on more than 10,000 interception videos.

An unnamed Brave1 fixed-wing interceptor (MaXon, per the NYT via DroneXL) costs about $3,500; the operator selects the target "in software, one click", after which it is 95% automated from launch to kill; it was first used in combat in Kharkiv oblast in June 2026.

Project Eagle's Merops (Surveyor) interceptor flies at over 280 km/h, costs about $15,000, is catapult-launched and one-way, has a crew of 3–4 (pilot, navigator, explosives technician, launcher and antenna engineer), and its own sensor "illuminates and locks onto the target from a distance"; it has been in Ukraine since May 2025.

cites.quote: illuminates and locks onto the target from a distance

text: NOCTIS/Vyriy's ZIRKA interceptor is claimed to fly at 340+ km/h with a 30 km radius and 20 minutes' endurance, to cost up to $2,000, and to detect, track and guide automatically.
The Last Shadow T200 interceptor flies at 300 km/h for 1 hour and hops video channels against Russian "Shtora" image spoofing.
The maker of the General Chereshnya AIR interceptor says it downed Gerberas in July 2025.

Ukrainian interceptor crews in a van watch radar dots and steer the interceptor toward one until the Shahed appears on the drone's camera, then fly into it; they have "a few minutes" from the Shahed appearing on radar until it leaves range.
A ground radar cue plus a pilot who takes manual control for the final seconds is the norm for Ukrainian interceptor drones, and performance "depends on good radar cueing and trained pilots".

cites.quote: depends on good radar cueing and trained pilots

text: A Merops crew member says the most accurate target data comes from "a calibrated radar with a competent operator", while flight-path programmes can be off by about a kilometre.

cites.quote: a calibrated radar with a competent operator

metric_new.label: Position error of a target cue

notes: A crew's statement, not a measured accuracy.

text: A Merops crew member says the previous Ukrainian interceptor had to search for its target from about 200 m with a poorer camera, whereas Merops's own sensor locks on from further out.
notes: A crew's statement, not a measured accuracy.

text: Wild Hornets gives 10–15 seconds from detection to kill for the Sting, and says 8 in 10 kills need only one interceptor.

observations.subject: Sting kills needing only one interceptor

text: Merops crews' best shifts in 2026 were 47 kills with 54 drones and 32 kills with 34 drones; a ground station needs at least 32 interceptors a month.
A Ukrainian platoon commander's rule is: "Even if you use 50 drones to shoot down one Shahed, it's worth it".

cites.quote: Even if you use 50 drones to shoot down one Shahed, it's worth it

observations.subject: hypothetical interceptors per Shahed still worth it

text: In 2026 the human role in Ukrainian interceptor drones narrowed to selecting a target and authorising the strike.
No one on the record has said how per-target human authorisation of autonomous interceptors copes with hundreds of Shaheds arriving at once.
The first known Sting interceptor appeared in October 2024.
Ukrainian interceptor drones made their first kills of Shaheds in early 2025.
Zelensky said interceptor drones downed "dozens" of drones in a 500-drone Russian attack in July 2025.
On 30 November 2025 Stings made their first kills of jet Geran-3s, downing several of 138 launched.
notes: The table does not say whether 138 counts only Geran-3s or the whole attack.

text: Beskrestnov put interceptor drones' share of Shahed kills at about 10% in winter 2025–26.
notes: Disagrees with Reuters' about 25% for the same winter.

text: Reuters put interceptor drones' share of Shahed kills at about 25% in winter 2025–26.
notes: Disagrees with Beskrestnov's about 10% for the same winter.

text: In February 2026 Ukrainian interceptor drones flew about 6,300 sorties and made more than 1,500 kills, about 70% of them near Kyiv.

observations.subject: share of interceptor kills near Kyiv

text: In April 2026 interceptor drones made about 40% of Ukraine's Shahed-type kills, with about 1,000 crews.
In May 2026 Beskrestnov put interceptor drones at about 50% of Shahed kills, and Syrskyi said the Unmanned Systems Forces made more than 1,200 interceptor kills.
In May 2026 the Sting's maker claimed more than 3,000 kills.
One Ukrainian interceptor crew logged ten launches in a night and found no Shahed, and on a foggy March night Kharkiv crews aborted because the cameras saw nothing.

observations.subject: one crew, one night, no Shahed found

text: Merops crews say "no camera has yet handled bad weather well", though one pilot flying manually intercepted in hail, snow and fog.

cites.quote: No camera has yet handled bad weather well

text: Heavy snow or rain can keep mobile fire groups' interceptor drones on the ground.
When Shaheds sped up from about 170 to over 200 km/h, the first Ukrainian interceptor became ineffective within four months, and interceptors were upgraded to about 300 km/h.
Jet Gerans at 300–600 km/h outrun Ukraine's propeller interceptor drones.
The Geran-3 cruised at only 300–350 km/h to save fuel and sprinted near known air defences, which let Stings catch some.
The first "ready" Ukrainian jet interceptors failed for lack of machine-vision lock, loiter fuel and agility.
Merops crews say jet Gerans slow when they manoeuvre and can lose control under EW, and one jet fell after five attempts with an ordinary interceptor.

observations.subject: ordinary interceptor against one jet Geran

text: From November 2025 Shaheds carried rear-view cameras above and below the hull, with extra tail antennas, apparently to see an interceptor entering the rear sector and manoeuvre.
Shahed evasion manoeuvres introduced in July–August 2025 took Ukrainian engineers about two weeks to counter.
The Russian "Shtora" system spoofs Ukrainian interceptor drones' video.
Pilot training is a bottleneck for Ukrainian interceptor drones.
Some Ukrainian interceptor crews did not update ground-station firmware, and some makers' drones flew poorly.

In April 2025 Celebra Tech claimed its Tryzub laser destroys FPVs, bombs and missiles to 3 km, Shaheds, helicopters and aircraft to 5 km, and dazzles to 10 km; its power is classified, it is aimed by an operator with a joystick, no engagement was cited and its service date is unknown.

observations.subject: Tryzub against FPVs, bombs and missiles
Tryzub against Shaheds, helicopters and aircraft

text: In May 2026 USF commander Sukharevskyi said of Tryzub: "at altitude over 2 km we can already shoot down aircraft with this laser"; earlier it had burned FPVs and damaged reconnaissance UAV optics at up to 1,500 m.

cites.quote: at altitude over 2 km we can already shoot down aircraft with this laser

metric_new.label: Maximum effective engagement altitude of a weapon

observations.subject: Tryzub against FPVs and reconnaissance UAV optics

text: In the May 2026 Tryzub video the laser was aimed by hand and automatic tracking was not visible; analysts call it a functional prototype, with no cost or production plan.
In July 2026 Deputy Commander-in-Chief Lebedenko said of Tryzub: "It can already shoot down FPVs today, it is already working today on Shaheds", and promised laser air defence in 2–3 months.

cites.quote: It can already shoot down FPVs today, it is already working today on Shaheds

text: As of July 2026 there was no documented Shahed kill by Tryzub, and the date for laser air defence has slipped repeatedly.
In February 2026 the Sunray prototype, a telescope-like unit on a pickup, burned a small drone in seconds, silently and with no visible beam, as The Atlantic reported and DroneXL relayed.
The Sunray laser's cost is given as "a few hundred thousand dollars" or "a few million"; the article conflicts.
In June 2024 the Ukrainian Air Force commander said mobile fire groups would likely add interceptor operators and "combat lasers".
Lasers need line of sight, lose power in cloud, rain, smoke and dust, and must hold the beam on a moving target.
No source was found of a Ukrainian high-power microwave or EMP system used against Shaheds; the only figure found is a vendor's claim of about $0.05 per microwave shot, in a US cost survey.
Ukraine's national GNSS jamming and spoofing system, Pokrova (mostly Lima), has been operating since early 2024.
Lima's maker claims more than 20,500 Shaheds jammed.
Lima's operators claim about half of all "intercepted" Shaheds and missiles.

observations.subject: Lima's share of intercepted Shaheds and missiles

text: On 4 July 2025, of 539 Russian drones and decoys, 268 were shot down, 208 were "diverted (likely by Ukrainian jamming)" and 63 struck.
Reuters says Ukrainian EW can neutralise nearly half of a Russian drone attack on some nights, but its effect varies.

observations.subject: share of an attack neutralised by EW on some nights

text: Trench Art argues jammers are the only truly cost-effective defence against Shaheds.
Chinese CRPA antennas appeared on Shaheds in January 2025 with 8 elements, then 16 by March 2025, and Russia's 12-element Kometa was found on a Shahed in February 2025.
Ihnat said: "The more antennas the drone has, the more suppression systems we need".

cites.quote: The more antennas the drone has, the more suppression systems we need

text: The CRPA ladder on Russian strike drones continued to 32 elements in 2026.
Ihnat says some Shaheds carry cameras, SIM cards, modems or Starlink, which makes them harder to jam, steerable online and usable as relays for other drones.
Mesh modems followed on Russian Shaheds in 2025–26.

In November 2024 Ukrainian GNSS spoofing moved Ukrainians' phones into Moscow, Bryansk, Kursk and Belgorod, shifted their clocks to Russian time and disrupted taxis and maps; the General Staff advised turning off automatic time.

mentions.name: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine

text: At the front, Ukrainian brigade commanders banned Lima-Quant because it blinded their own Mavics.
Mobile EW teams with Nota rode with Ukrainian mobile fire groups from 2023.
CSIS estimates a Shahed-136/Geran-2 costs $20,000–50,000, with a midpoint of $35,000.
2022 reporting put a Shahed-136 at about $20,000.
The export version of the Shahed costs about $193,000, and the Russian-made version $10,000–50,000.
CSIS estimates the Shahed's cost per target struck at about $350,000.
A .50 cal round is estimated to cost $2.67–7.
A 35 mm Gepard round costs about $600; Germany's $181m for 300,000 rounds works out at about $603 a round.
A Gepard's cost per Shahed is "a few thousand dollars"; 7–30 rounds at $600 is about $4,000–18,000 (computed).

metric_new.label: Defender cost per aerial target killed
Defender cost per aerial target killed

text: A 35 mm AHEAD round for Skynex costs about €1,120 (about $1,290), derived from a Romanian contract.
Skynex's cost per target is reported as "just over $4,000" (2024) but derived as about $12,900 per 10-round burst; the two disagree.

metric_new.label: Defender cost per aerial target killed
Defender cost per aerial target killed

text: Maker or official figures put interceptor drones at under $1,500 for the cheapest, about $1,000 for P1-SUN, about $2,000–2,500 for Sting, about $3,500 for MaXon and about $15,000 for Merops.
An APKWS II rocket costs about $30,000–31,000, according to contracts.
An IRIS-T missile costs about $450,000, a NASAMS missile $600,000–1m and a Patriot missile nearly $4m.
David Axe puts the LMM (Martlet) at more than $500,000 per missile, with a mass of 13 kg and a reach of 8 km.
A laser shot costs "mainly electricity", and a vendor claims under $5 per shot.
In 2022 a US officer called using fighters against $20,000 drones "completely wasteful".

text: Russia answered Ukrainian GNSS spoofing with CRPA antennas on Shaheds, going from 8 to 16 elements between January and March 2025.
In 2025 (e8a) Shaheds flew above 2 km with a terminal dive and waves were 40% decoys; Ukraine answered with interceptor drones (first Shahed kills early 2025) and F-16 patrols.

In July–November 2025 Russia answered Ukrainian interceptors with rear cameras and evasion on Shaheds, used scouting and guided Shaheds against mobile fire groups, and put MANPADS and R-60 missiles on Shaheds against helicopters.
In late 2025–spring 2026 (e8b–e9a) Russia flew mass piston-engined waves, 8,161 in May 2026.
In late 2025–spring 2026 Ukraine's counter was interceptor drones at about 50% of kills, AI terminal lock and APKWS rockets on F-16s.
Russia answered Ukrainian interceptor drones with jet Gerans at 300–600 km/h and mesh radio.
In mid-2026 (e9b) jet Gerans were "beyond" Ukraine's interceptors and mobile fire groups, leaving missiles and fighters as the counter, with jet interceptors in testing and lasers promised.
